title: Interview Questions That Work
intro: Juniors used to write leading questions. Prompt-engineering habits have swung them to the opposite problem: flat, context-free questions that produce flat answers.

learn.title: Two failure modes
learn.text:
**Leading (the old problem)** — “How much do you love the new dashboard?”, example answers inside the question, two questions in one.

**Over-neutral (the new one)** — no scenario or moment in time, the same emotional temperature throughout, a rigid 15-question script that reads like an AI prompt.

Neutrality is one tool, not the goal.

try.q: What is the newer failure mode in interview guides?
options: Questions asked in the wrong order

learn.title: How to structure the guide
learn.text:
**Don't over-script.** Five broad questions organised by theme beat ten narrow ones. Follow relevant tangents — that's where discoveries are.

**Funnel.** Broad context first, then narrow to specifics.

**One question at a time.** Split double-barrelled questions; people answer only half.

**No example answers.** They anchor the response and shape what follows.

try.q: What happens when you ask a double-barrelled question?
options: People answer only half of it
People ask you to repeat it
People give a more detailed answer

learn.title: Framing on purpose
learn.text:
Add an **“if any” escape hatch**: “What problems, if any, did you run into?” lets people say “none” without feeling they've failed you.

And deliberate framing is legitimate when a follow-up needs focus: naming a specific moment or scenario is how experienced researchers direct a session without leading it.

try.q: What does “if any” do in a question?
options: Makes the question more neutral overall
try.explain: It removes the pressure to produce a problem.

options: Easy questions first, hard ones last
test.explain: It gives the specifics somewhere to sit.

test.q: Why avoid example answers in a question?
test.explain: And they shape every follow-up that comes after.

test.q: How many broad questions does Calabro suggest over ten narrow ones?
test.explain: Organised by theme, with room to follow tangents.

test.q: Where do discoveries usually come from?
test.explain: Which is why over-scripting costs you.

options: Yes, it always leads the participant
Only when the sample is small
